companies.name: Meta
companies.description: Largest XR platform player by volume — Quest headsets plus the Ray-Ban partnership line, spanning camera-only smart glasses through to display-equipped AR glasses.

news_log.text: Vision Pro (current shipping model) now runs the M5 chip (up from M2) with a dedicated R1 sensor chip, up to 120Hz refresh, ~10% more rendered pixels, up to 2x faster AI workloads. No mention of Vision Air or smart glasses on the official product page (expected -- companies don't pre-announce cancellations there); the Ternus/Vision Products Group pivot story remains tracked signal, not confirmed via official channels.

technologies.name: World Models
technologies.description: AI models that learn to simulate and predict how an environment evolves, rather than just perceiving it — e.g. Google DeepMind's Genie line. Relevant to XR as a possible foundation for scene understanding, content generation, and predictive rendering in future AR/VR systems.
technologies.tradeoffs: Still largely research-stage; not yet a shipping component in consumer XR hardware.
technologies.news: No tracked XR product embodies this yet — mapped to Google given DeepMind's Genie world-model research, not a specific device. Revisit if a product ships that uses it.

technologies.name: Waveguide Displays
technologies.description: Optical combiner that pipes a projected image through a thin, mostly-transparent lens to the eye via total internal reflection and diffraction gratings. The dominant approach for slim, glasses-like AR form factors.
technologies.tradeoffs: Enables the thinnest, most normal-looking glasses, but historically trades off against field of view, brightness/efficiency, and color uniformity (rainbow artifacts) compared to birdbath optics.

technologies.name: Birdbath Optics
technologies.description: Optical combiner using a beamsplitter and curved mirror (like looking into a birdbath) to reflect a projected image into the eye. Generally easier to manufacture with better color accuracy than early waveguides.
technologies.tradeoffs: Bulkier optical module than waveguides, making it harder to fit into a normal-glasses form factor — better suited to slightly thicker AR devices.
technologies.news: Mapped to Rokid Max — verify exact optical design terminology (birdbath vs. freeform prism) against an official source.

technologies.name: SLAM / VPS
technologies.description: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (building a map of the environment while tracking the device's position within it) and Visual Positioning System (using camera imagery to localize against a known map). The core technology that lets AR/MR devices anchor content to real-world surfaces.
technologies.tradeoffs: Accuracy and drift depend heavily on camera/sensor quality and lighting conditions; VPS additionally requires a pre-built map of the space to localize against.

technologies.name: ToF (Time-of-Flight)
technologies.description: Active depth sensing: a sensor emits light pulses and measures return time to build a depth map. Used for hand tracking, room/surface mapping, and passthrough depth in VR/MR headsets.
technologies.tradeoffs: Adds power draw and a dedicated sensor/emitter versus purely camera-based (passive) depth estimation; performance can degrade outdoors in bright sunlight.
technologies.news: Corrected: Apple Vision Pro's depth sensor is specifically a LiDAR Scanner per Apple's spec sheet (see lidar-scanning), not generic ToF — moved off this entry. Quest 3's depth sensor is commonly described as ToF; needs re-verification against an official Meta source.

technologies.name: UWB (Ultra-Wideband)
technologies.description: Radio technology for precise, short-range ranging and positioning (centimeter-level), already used for device-finding (AirTag, SmartTag) and increasingly explored for spatial anchors and object tracking in XR.
technologies.tradeoffs: Short range and requires UWB radios in both the device and whatever it's tracking against — not a standalone solution for room-scale AR tracking on its own.
technologies.news: No tracked product or company confidently confirmed using UWB for XR positioning specifically (vs. Find My / AirTag-style device-finding) — left unmapped rather than forcing a weak connection.

technologies.name: GNSS
technologies.description: Global Navigation Satellite System (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, etc.) — outdoor global positioning. Anchors AR content to real-world geolocation when a device is outside, complementing SLAM/VPS which works best for local, indoor tracking.
technologies.tradeoffs: Only accurate to a few meters and doesn't work indoors — needs SLAM/VPS or UWB for anything requiring precise local tracking.
technologies.news: No tracked product confirmed using GNSS for outdoor AR anchoring yet — left unmapped rather than forcing a weak connection.

technologies.name: Gaussian Splatting
technologies.description: 3D scene reconstruction and rendering technique that represents a scene as millions of colored, translucent 3D "splats" (Gaussians) fit from photos or video, then rendered in real time. Increasingly used for photorealistic 3D capture and novel-view synthesis.
technologies.tradeoffs: Much faster to render than traditional NeRFs and photorealistic from captured footage, but scenes are captured/reconstructed rather than fully editable 3D models — better suited to viewing/walkthroughs than asset pipelines needing traditional geometry.
technologies.news: No tracked product or company confirmed using Gaussian Splatting specifically (Matterport's pipeline is LiDAR + photogrammetry-based, not confirmed as Gaussian Splat) — left unmapped rather than forcing a weak connection.

technologies.name: VLE (unconfirmed)
technologies.description: Placeholder entry — Jenn listed "UWB/VLE/GNSS" as positioning technologies to track, but VLE's exact meaning wasn't confirmed. Possibly BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy)? Needs Jenn to confirm before this entry is filled in properly.
technologies.news: Stub entry pending clarification from Jenn on what VLE stands for.

technologies.name: Pancake Lenses
technologies.description: Folded optical design using polarization to fold the light path, allowing much thinner and lighter VR headsets than traditional Fresnel lenses.
technologies.tradeoffs: Requires polarized light (some brightness loss vs. Fresnel) but enables a dramatically slimmer headset.

technologies.name: Micro-OLED
technologies.description: Extremely high pixel-density OLED displays fabricated on a silicon backplane, used for the sharp, high-contrast displays in premium MR headsets.
technologies.tradeoffs: Excellent contrast and pixel density, but expensive to manufacture at scale and historically limited in peak brightness for outdoor AR use.

technologies.name: Micro-LED
technologies.description: Emerging self-emissive display technology using microscopic LEDs per pixel — the leading contender for bright, efficient, sunlight-readable AR glasses displays.
technologies.tradeoffs: Much brighter and more power-efficient than OLED/LCoS at small sizes, but mass production at the pixel pitch AR glasses need remains difficult and costly.
technologies.news: Meta Orion is reported to use micro-LED projectors — needs re-verification against an official source.

technologies.name: LCoS (Liquid Crystal on Silicon)
technologies.description: Reflective microdisplay technology commonly used as the image source (light engine) that projects into a waveguide combiner.
technologies.tradeoffs: Mature and relatively cheap, but less efficient and dimmer than newer micro-LED light engines.
technologies.news: Seed entry — verify Google Glass Enterprise Edition's light engine spec.

technologies.name: IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit)
technologies.description: Accelerometer + gyroscope (often + magnetometer) measuring orientation and motion at very low latency. Fused with camera-based SLAM/VPS for fast, drift-corrected head and hand tracking.
technologies.tradeoffs: Extremely low latency and cheap, but drifts over time on its own — needs fusion with visual tracking for long-term accuracy.

technologies.name: Eye Tracking
technologies.description: Cameras and IR illuminators inside the headset track gaze direction and pupil position, enabling foveated rendering, gaze-based UI input, and iris authentication.
technologies.tradeoffs: Enables major rendering/interaction gains but adds sensors, power draw, and calibration requirements.

technologies.name: Hand Tracking
technologies.description: Camera-based skeletal tracking of hands and fingers, enabling controller-free interaction in VR/MR.
technologies.tradeoffs: Removes the need for physical controllers but is generally less precise and more occlusion-prone than controller-based tracking.

technologies.name: Structured Light
technologies.description: Depth sensing by projecting a known light pattern and measuring its distortion on surfaces — an alternative to Time-of-Flight for close-range depth capture.
technologies.tradeoffs: Very accurate at short range but generally less effective outdoors in bright light than ToF.

technologies.name: NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields)
technologies.description: Earlier neural technique for reconstructing a 3D scene from photos and rendering novel viewpoints — largely the predecessor to Gaussian Splatting.
technologies.tradeoffs: Very high visual quality, but historically far slower to train and render than Gaussian Splatting, which has displaced it for most real-time use cases.
technologies.news: No tracked product or company confirmed using NeRF directly — mostly of historical/comparative interest now that Gaussian Splatting dominates real-time use. Left unmapped rather than forcing a weak connection.

technologies.name: Photogrammetry
technologies.description: Classical technique for reconstructing 3D geometry and texture from overlapping photographs, without neural rendering.
technologies.tradeoffs: Produces traditional, editable 3D meshes (unlike Gaussian Splats/NeRFs), but is more labor-intensive and can struggle with reflective or textureless surfaces.
technologies.news: Matterport Pro3 (previously linked here) actually uses LiDAR + spherical photo capture, not classic photogrammetry -- corrected 2026-09-27. No tracked product confirmed using true photogrammetry -- left unmapped rather than forcing a weak connection.

technologies.name: LiDAR Scanning
technologies.description: Direct laser time-of-flight depth capture used in phones and dedicated scanners for fast room- and object-scale 3D scanning.
technologies.tradeoffs: Fast and works in low light or on texture-less surfaces (unlike photogrammetry), but lower resolution than photogrammetry or Gaussian Splatting for fine detail.

technologies.name: Foveated Rendering
technologies.description: Renders full detail only where the eye is looking (via eye tracking) and reduces detail in peripheral vision, cutting GPU load substantially.
technologies.tradeoffs: Major performance win, but requires accurate, low-latency eye tracking to avoid visible quality loss.

technologies.name: Passthrough / Video See-Through
technologies.description: Cameras on the outside of a headset feed a live video view of the real world, composited with virtual content — as opposed to optical see-through (waveguide/birdbath), which lets real light through directly.
technologies.tradeoffs: Enables full mixed reality on a VR-style headset without waveguide optics, but adds latency and processing load versus true optical see-through, and image quality is capped by the outward-facing cameras.

technologies.name: Split / Edge Rendering
technologies.description: Offloads the heaviest rendering work to a phone, PC, or cloud server and streams frames to lightweight glasses, keeping the wearable device thin and low-power.
technologies.tradeoffs: Enables much lighter glasses, but depends on a fast, low-latency connection to the compute source — no phone/PC nearby degrades or breaks the experience.

technologies.name: Wi-Fi 6E / 7
technologies.description: High-bandwidth, low-latency wireless standards used for tethered-feeling wireless VR (e.g. streaming PC VR to a standalone headset).
technologies.tradeoffs: Enables cable-free high-fidelity streaming, but performance depends on a strong, congestion-free local network.
technologies.news: Quest 3 supports Wi-Fi 6E for Air Link-style wireless PC VR streaming — needs re-verification of exact spec.

technologies.name: 5G / mmWave
technologies.description: Cellular connectivity fast enough to support cloud-rendered AR/VR content streamed to lightweight glasses on the go, rather than tethered to a local phone or PC.
technologies.tradeoffs: Removes the need for a nearby compute device, but mmWave has short range/poor building penetration, and cloud round-trip latency remains a challenge for real-time interaction.
technologies.news: No tracked product ships this yet — mapped to Qualcomm as the chipset company driving 5G+XR convergence (Snapdragon XR platforms), not a specific device.

technologies.name: Bluetooth LE Audio
technologies.description: Lower-power, higher-quality Bluetooth audio standard relevant to the open-ear audio in camera/audio smart glasses like Ray-Ban Meta.
technologies.tradeoffs: Better battery life and multi-stream support than classic Bluetooth audio, but requires both device and earbuds/glasses to support the newer standard.
technologies.news: Verify Ray-Ban Meta's actual Bluetooth audio spec version.

technologies.name: EMG (Electromyography) Input
technologies.description: Wristband sensors read electrical signals from forearm muscles to detect subtle finger/hand gestures as an input method, without needing the hand to be in camera view.
technologies.tradeoffs: Works even when hands are out of camera view or in a pocket, but is an early-stage/prototype technology with a smaller software ecosystem than camera-based hand tracking.

technologies.name: Haptic Feedback
technologies.description: Vests, gloves, or controllers that simulate touch and force feedback for virtual objects and impacts.
technologies.tradeoffs: Adds meaningful immersion for VR, but adds cost, bulk, and another device to wear/charge.

technologies.name: On-Device Multimodal AI
technologies.description: Local AI models running directly on glasses/headsets for real-time scene understanding, translation, and voice assistants without a round-trip to the cloud.
technologies.tradeoffs: Lower latency and works offline, but constrained by the device's compute/battery budget compared to cloud-hosted models.
technologies.news: Verify which specific features actually run on-device vs. cloud on current Ray-Ban Meta hardware.

technologies.name: OLEDoS (OLED-on-Silicon)
technologies.description: OLED microdisplay fabricated on a silicon backplane rather than glass — the specific manufacturing approach a handful of vendors (Samsung Display, Sony, eMagin) specialize in for near-eye displays.
technologies.tradeoffs: Often used interchangeably with "Micro-OLED" in casual coverage, but OLEDoS specifically denotes the silicon-backplane fabrication process; kept as a distinct entry since Samsung Display's own materials use the OLEDoS term specifically.
technologies.news: Corrected 2026-09-27: Samsung Galaxy Glasses actually have NO built-in display (audio-only) per news.samsung.com -- the earlier OLEDoS microdisplay assumption was wrong. Left unmapped pending a real product that confirms OLEDoS use.

technologies.name: Mini-LED
technologies.description: LED backlight technology using thousands of small LEDs with local dimming zones for high contrast and brightness -- distinct from Micro-LED (which is self-emissive per-pixel). Used in high-end enterprise headsets for HDR-grade contrast.
technologies.tradeoffs: Much better contrast/brightness than standard LCD backlighting and cheaper to manufacture at scale than Micro-LED, but still not per-pixel emissive like OLED/Micro-LED -- can show blooming around bright objects on a dark background.
